doctrines.name: Mission and the Religions
doctrines.question: What is the Church sent to do, and how does Christ relate to the world’s religions?
doctrines.summary: From the Great Commission and Justin’s "seeds of the Word" to Jesuit accommodation and the Chinese Rites, the Protestant missionary movement, the three-self principle, Vatican II, Lausanne and the southward shift of Christianity, this section traces debates over mission, culture, colonialism, religious liberty and the salvation of non-Christians.
doctrines.longText:
The risen Christ sent his followers to make disciples of all nations, and within three centuries the faith had spread from Ireland to India and Ethiopia. From the start Christians held two convictions in tension. One was that there is "none other name" by which people are saved. The other was that God had "not left himself without witness" among the nations. Justin Martyr saw seeds of the divine Word in Socrates. Cyprian taught that there is no salvation outside the Church, and the Council of Florence (1442) applied the maxim strictly. Missionary practice was just as varied. Gregory the Great told missionaries to convert pagan temples rather than destroy them. The Church of the East presented Christ in Buddhist and Daoist idiom in Tang China. Spanish conquest tied baptism to the sword, and Las Casas protested that faith can only be offered by persuasion.

In the 17th century the Jesuits Ricci and de Nobili adopted Chinese and Indian dress, language and thought. The Chinese Rites controversy ended with papal bans (1704–1742) that crippled the mission until they were reversed in 1939. William Carey (1792) launched the Protestant missionary movement, which planted churches across Asia, Africa and the Pacific, often in the shadow of empire. Henry Venn and John Nevius urged self-supporting, self-governing, self-propagating churches, but paternalism often blocked them, as in the treatment of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther. The Edinburgh conference of 1910 dreamed of evangelising the world in a generation and gave birth to the ecumenical movement.

The 20th century reframed both mission and the religions. At Tambaram (1938) Kraemer argued that the gospel stands in discontinuity with all religions. Willingen (1952) grounded mission in the missio Dei, the sending of the triune God. Rahner proposed "anonymous Christians", Vatican II taught respect for what is "true and holy" in other faiths and affirmed religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae, 1965), and John Hick called for a pluralist "Copernican revolution". Evangelicals at Lausanne (1974) reaffirmed Christ’s uniqueness and, prompted by Latin Americans, integral mission. They later divided between restrictivism and a "wider hope". Meanwhile Christianity’s centre of gravity moved to the Global South. Andrew Walls and Lamin Sanneh argued that the translatable gospel had escaped its colonial carriers, and missionaries now go out from Seoul, Lagos and São Paulo. Each position is presented here in its own terms, with its strongest critics.

nodes.label: What is the Church sent to do, and how does Christ relate to the world’s religions?
nodes.text: Jesus sent his disciples to "teach all nations", and the apostles proclaimed that "there is none other name under heaven" by which we must be saved. Yet Paul told the Athenians that God "left not himself without witness". Must people hear of Christ to be saved? How should missionaries treat other cultures and religions? Was modern mission the servant of empire or the seed of world Christianity?

nodes.label: The Great Commission (Matt 28:18–20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)
nodes.text: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them ... teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." The risen Christ sends his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth".

nodes.label: "None other name" (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Tim 2:5)
nodes.text: "No man cometh unto the Father, but by me"; "neither is there salvation in any other"; "one mediator between God and men". Exclusivists read these as requiring explicit faith; inclusivists as saying that all who are saved are saved by Christ.

nodes.label: God’s witness among the nations (Acts 14:17; 17:22–31; Rom 1:19–20; 2:14–16)
nodes.text: At Lystra and Athens Paul speaks of the God who "left not himself without witness", quotes pagan poets and finds an altar "to the unknown god"; Romans speaks of creation’s testimony and a law written on Gentile hearts, yet also of humanity "without excuse".

nodes.label: Every nation, tribe and tongue (Gen 12:3; Rev 7:9; 21:24–26)
nodes.text: God’s promise that in Abraham "all families of the earth" will be blessed ends in a multitude from "all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" and the glory of the nations brought into the New Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Justin: seeds of the Word among the Greeks (c.155)
nodes.text: Justin holds that the divine Logos sowed seeds of truth in every people, so that Socrates and others who lived by reason were in a sense Christians before Christ: an early source for inclusivist thought.

nodes.label: Cyprian: no salvation outside the Church (c.256)
nodes.text: In the rebaptism dispute Cyprian insists that grace and salvation are found only within the one Church; the maxim extra ecclesiam nulla salus becomes a pillar of later teaching.

nodes.label: Gregory the Great: convert the temples, not destroy them (601)
nodes.text: Writing to the mission to the English, Gregory advises that pagan temples be purified and reused and festivals turned to Christian feasts, because people rise "by degrees": a classic text of missionary adaptation.

nodes.label: The Church of the East in Tang China (635–781)
nodes.text: East Syriac missionaries from Persia reach Chang’an (635); the Xi’an Stele (781) presents the "Luminous Religion" in Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary. Their creative translation has been praised as early inculturation and criticised as syncretism.

nodes.label: Restrictivism: explicit faith and membership required (Florence, 1442)
nodes.text: The Council of Florence’s decree for the Copts (Cantate Domino, 1442) declares that pagans, Jews, heretics and schismatics outside the Catholic Church cannot share eternal life unless joined to it before death. Many Protestants likewise held that only those who hear and believe the gospel are saved.

nodes.label: Conquest and conversion in the Americas (1492–1550)
nodes.text: The papal bulls of 1493 and the Spanish Requerimiento (1513), read to Indigenous peoples before attack, tie evangelisation to conquest; mass baptisms follow violence, enslavement and epidemic. Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits also build schools, hospitals and Indigenous-language literature.

nodes.label: Las Casas: the gospel must be offered by persuasion, not force (1537–1550)
nodes.text: Bartolomé de las Casas argues (The Only Way, c.1537) that faith must be freely embraced, and at Valladolid (1550–51) defends Indigenous rights against Sepúlveda’s case for just war and "natural slavery".

nodes.label: Jesuit accommodation: Ricci and de Nobili (1601–1610)
nodes.text: Matteo Ricci adopts the dress of a Confucian scholar, uses the classics to speak of the "Lord of Heaven", and treats ancestor and Confucius rites as civil honours; Roberto de Nobili lives as a Brahmin ascetic in Madurai.

nodes.label: Rome bans the Chinese Rites (1704–1742)
nodes.text: After protests by Dominicans and Franciscans, Clement XI condemns the rites (1704; Ex illa die, 1715) and Benedict XIV’s Ex quo singulari (1742) ends debate. The Kangxi Emperor responds by restricting the mission. Pius XII reverses the ban in 1939.

nodes.label: William Carey and the Protestant missionary movement (1792)
nodes.text: Carey’s Enquiry and the Baptist Missionary Society launch a wave of voluntary societies (LMS 1795, CMS 1799, ABCFM 1810); Carey’s Serampore team translates the Bible into dozens of Indian languages.

nodes.label: The indigenous principle: self-supporting, self-governing, self-propagating (1850s–1890)
nodes.text: Henry Venn (CMS) and Rufus Anderson (ABCFM) set the goal of "three-self" churches; John Nevius’s plan (1886, adopted in Korea from 1890) and Roland Allen’s Missionary Methods (1912) press local leadership from the start.

nodes.label: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, first African Anglican bishop (1864)
nodes.text: A rescued Yoruba slave, Crowther is consecrated bishop of the Niger (1864), the fruit of Venn’s policy; in the 1880s younger European missionaries undermine his mission, and he is succeeded by a European, a turning point in African disillusionment with missionary paternalism.

nodes.label: Mission and empire: the high imperial age (1880–1914)
nodes.text: The Berlin Conference (1884–85) partitions Africa; missions often rely on colonial protection and share racial assumptions. Critics from Gandhi to postcolonial historians portray mission as cultural imperialism; others show missionaries opposing slavery, forced labour and settler abuses.

nodes.label: Edinburgh World Missionary Conference (1910)
nodes.text: Some 1,200 delegates (only about 20 from Asia and none from Africa) plan the "evangelization of the world in this generation" under John R. Mott; the conference births the International Missionary Council (1921) and the ecumenical movement.

nodes.label: Particularism: Kraemer at Tambaram (1938)
nodes.text: At the IMC meeting in Tambaram, India, Hendrik Kraemer, influenced by Barth, argues for the "discontinuity" of the gospel with all religions; Indian Christians such as P. Chenchiah protest that this ignores God’s work in Indian religious life.

nodes.label: Rome rejects strict extra ecclesiam (1949)
nodes.text: The Holy Office letter on Leonard Feeney teaches that those invincibly ignorant of the Church may be saved by an implicit desire informed by charity, opening the way to Vatican II’s inclusivism.

nodes.label: Missio Dei: mission belongs to God (Willingen, 1952)
nodes.text: After the expulsion of missionaries from China, the IMC at Willingen roots mission in the Trinity: the Father sends the Son, the Father and Son send the Spirit, and the triune God sends the Church. Later ecumenical versions stress God’s work in history and "humanisation".

nodes.label: China’s Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954)
nodes.text: The communist state adopts the three-self language to cut churches off from foreign missions under party oversight; unregistered house churches resist. Ironically, Chinese Protestantism grows from under one million (1949) to tens of millions without missionaries.

nodes.label: Inclusivism: "anonymous Christians" (Rahner, 1961)
nodes.text: Karl Rahner argues that God’s universal saving will means grace is offered to all, including through other religions; those who accept it are saved by Christ as "anonymous Christians".

nodes.label: Vatican II on the religions and mission (1964–65)
nodes.text: Lumen Gentium 16 says those who without fault do not know Christ but seek God sincerely may attain salvation; Nostra Aetate (1965) says the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions; Ad Gentes reaffirms the missionary nature of the Church.

nodes.label: Religious liberty: Dignitatis Humanae (1965)
nodes.text: The Council affirms freedom from coercion in religion as a right grounded in human dignity: a principle long defended by Anabaptists, Baptists (Thomas Helwys, Roger Williams) and Quakers, now embraced by the Catholic Church and the WCC.

nodes.label: Pluralism: Hick’s "Copernican revolution" (1973)
nodes.text: John Hick proposes that the world religions are equally valid responses to one ultimate Reality; Paul Knitter, Wilfred Cantwell Smith and Stanley Samartha develop pluralist and liberationist versions.

nodes.label: Lausanne Covenant and integral mission (1974)
nodes.text: Evangelicals at Lausanne affirm the uniqueness of Christ and urgency of evangelism against universalism and pluralism, while Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar win recognition of social responsibility; "integral mission" and "unreached people groups" (Ralph Winter) both emerge.

nodes.label: Contextualisation and inculturation (1972–1979)
nodes.text: Shoki Coe coins "contextualisation" (1972); Paul VI’s Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) and Pedro Arrupe (1978) speak of evangelising cultures and "inculturation"; African theologians (John Mbiti, Kwame Bediako) and Asian theologians recover pre-Christian religious heritage as preparation for the gospel.

nodes.label: Translatability and world Christianity (Sanneh, Walls, 1989)
nodes.text: Lamin Sanneh and Andrew Walls argue that Bible translation made Christianity endlessly culturally translatable, so missions sowed vernacular renewal that escaped Western control; Robert Woodberry’s data (2012) link Protestant missions with literacy and democracy.

nodes.label: The wider hope among evangelicals (1992)
nodes.text: Clark Pinnock and John Sanders argue that the unevangelised may be saved by responding to the light they have; others propose post-mortem encounter with Christ. Ronald Nash and most confessional evangelicals defend restrictivism.

nodes.label: Objection: Dominus Iesus (2000)
nodes.text: The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith rejects pluralist theologies, affirms Christ as unique and universal saviour and the necessity of the Church, and investigates Jacques Dupuis’s inclusive pluralism (notified 2001).

nodes.label: The southward shift of Christianity (2000s)
nodes.text: By 2000 most Christians live in Africa, Asia and Latin America; Africa becomes the largest Christian continent by the 2010s. Walls, Sanneh, Philip Jenkins (The Next Christendom, 2002) and others describe "world Christianity" and "reverse mission" from South to North.

nodes.label: Today: who holds what?
nodes.text: Catholic teaching combines Christ’s unique mediation with Vatican II inclusivism and dialogue; Orthodox churches stress the Church as ark of salvation while leaving judgement of others to God; most evangelicals and Pentecostals hold particularism, divided between restrictivism and wider-hope views; liberal Protestants often embrace pluralism. Mission now flows from everywhere to everywhere: Korea, Brazil and Nigeria send thousands of missionaries, while debates over proselytism, conversion laws (e.g. in India) and religious liberty intensify.

positions.name: Great Commission evangelism (priority of evangelism)
altNames: Evangelization of the world in this generation
positions.oneLine: The church’s central mission is to proclaim Christ to every people so that they may repent, believe and be gathered into churches; this task remains binding on every generation and is urgent because people are lost without Christ.
coreClaims: The Great Commission binds the church until the end of the age (Matt 28:20).
Humanity is lost apart from Christ, so evangelism has priority, though not exclusivity, in the church’s mission.
Every "people group" (ethnos) must be reached; the gospel must be preached in all the world before the end (Matt 24:14).
Mission is the task of every believer, organised through voluntary societies and churches.
positions.origin: Practised from the apostles onward; given modern Protestant form by William Carey’s Enquiry (1792) and the missionary societies; amplified by Hudson Taylor, the Student Volunteer Movement ("the evangelization of the world in this generation", 1886), Edinburgh 1910, Lausanne 1974 (which said evangelism is primary) and Ralph Winter’s "unreached people groups" (1974).
strongestArguments: It takes the risen Christ’s last command at face value.
If salvation is through faith in Christ, love for neighbours requires telling them.
Its fruit is visible in the growth of churches in Korea, Africa, Latin America and among unreached peoples.
strongestObjections: Critics argue it reduces mission to verbal proclamation and neglects justice and service (an objection pressed by Latin American evangelicals at Lausanne).
Its alliance with Western power and culture produced paternalism and cultural imperialism.
Pluralists and many in other religions see conversion efforts as disrespectful or as proselytism.
responses: Defenders reply that evangelism and social care go together, but that only the gospel addresses humanity’s deepest need of reconciliation with God (Lausanne Covenant 6).
They point out that most missionaries today come from the Global South and that converts often embraced Christianity against colonial interests.
consequences: The modern missionary movement and the global spread of Protestantism.
Bible translation into over 700 complete languages.
Strategies such as people-group research, the 10/40 Window and church-planting movements.

positions.name: Accommodation (Jesuit method)
positions.oneLine: Missionaries should adapt to the language, dress, manners and intellectual traditions of a people, treating civil customs such as ancestral rites as compatible with Christianity, and presenting the gospel as the fulfilment of their best wisdom.
coreClaims: Grace perfects nature: truths in Confucian, Hindu and other traditions can be preparation for the gospel.
Missionaries should become "all things to all men", adopting local dress, language and etiquette.
Rites honouring ancestors and Confucius are civil and familial, not idolatrous worship.
Indigenous terms (Tian, Shangdi) can name the true God.
Conversion of elites can open whole societies to the faith.
positions.origin: Developed by Alessandro Valignano for Japan (1579), practised by Matteo Ricci in China (in Beijing from 1601) and Roberto de Nobili in India (from 1606); condemned in the Chinese Rites (1704–1742) and Malabar Rites (1704–1744) controversies; rehabilitated in 1939 and echoed by Vatican II.
strongestArguments: Paul at Athens quoted pagan poets and built on the "unknown god".
It won respected converts among Chinese literati and built a lasting Chinese Catholic community.
Treating filial piety as idolatry made conversion appear to require betraying one’s family and nation.
strongestObjections: Dominicans and Franciscans argued that ancestral rites included sacrifice and prayers to spirits, so tolerating them was syncretism.
Accepting caste distinctions in India (de Nobili) seemed to contradict Christian equality.
Elite-focused strategy depended on imperial favour and collapsed when it was withdrawn.
responses: Defenders noted that the Kangxi Emperor himself declared the rites civil (1700) and that Rome reversed its ban in 1939.
They argued that de Nobili distinguished social customs from religious ones and that later accommodation could correct abuses.
consequences: Chinese Rites controversy and the decline of the Qing-era mission.
Suppression of the Jesuits (1773) was hastened by these disputes.
Precedent for 20th-century inculturation.

positions.name: Inculturation and contextualisation
positions.oneLine: The gospel must be expressed through each culture’s language, symbols, music, thought-forms and social realities, so that Christ becomes at home among every people while also transforming their cultures.
coreClaims: The incarnation is the model: the Word took flesh in a particular culture.
No culture, including Western Christian culture, is normative; all are both affirmed and judged by the gospel.
Local theologies arise from the meeting of Scripture and context (Bevans’ "models of contextual theology").
Pre-Christian religious heritage can be a preparation for the gospel (Bediako, Mbiti).
Critical contextualisation tests customs by Scripture to avoid syncretism (Paul Hiebert).
positions.origin: The term "contextualization" was coined by Shoki Coe and Aharon Sapsezian in the Theological Education Fund (1972); "inculturation" was popularised by Jesuit superior Pedro Arrupe (1978) and John Paul II (Catechesi Tradendae, 1979) following Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975). Roots in early Syriac, Ethiopian and Celtic Christianity and in Jesuit accommodation.
strongestArguments: The Jerusalem council refused to impose Jewish culture on Gentile believers (Acts 15).
Christianity has always been translated into new cultures (Greek, Latin, Syriac, Slavic), so the principle is ancient.
Faith that remains foreign stays shallow; indigenous expression produces deep and lasting churches.
strongestObjections: Critics warn of syncretism, when culture rather than Scripture sets the agenda (e.g. accommodation to ancestor veneration or caste).
Some argue that "context" can be used to relativise doctrine and ethics (debates in the Anglican Communion).
Postcolonial critics note that outsiders often decide what counts as authentic local culture.
responses: Proponents distinguish critical contextualisation (Scripture judges culture) from uncritical accommodation.
They argue that every theology, including Western theology, is contextual, so the real choice is between conscious and unconscious contextualisation.
consequences: African, Asian and Latin American theologies; local music and art in worship.
Zaire Use of the Roman Rite (1988) and Indian Christian ashrams.
Debates over insider movements among Muslim-background believers.

positions.name: The indigenous ("three-self") principle
positions.oneLine: Missions should plant churches that are self-supporting, self-governing and self-propagating from as early as possible, with local leaders, so that the foreign mission can withdraw.
coreClaims: The goal of mission is a mature local church, not a permanent mission station.
Foreign money and control create dependency and stunt growth.
Local believers should evangelise their own people.
Paul’s practice of appointing elders and moving on is the model (Allen).
positions.origin: Formulated in the 1840s–50s by Henry Venn of the CMS and Rufus Anderson of the ABCFM; applied by John Nevius (Methods of Mission Work, 1886) and in Korea from 1890; advocated by Roland Allen (Missionary Methods: St Paul’s or Ours?, 1912). In China the terminology was co-opted by the state’s Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954).
strongestArguments: Korean Protestantism, built on the Nevius plan, became one of the strongest indigenous churches in Asia.
It follows Paul’s method of short stays and local elders.
It counters colonial paternalism by entrusting authority to local Christians.
strongestObjections: In practice missions often delayed handover for generations on paternalistic grounds (as in the undermining of Crowther).
The Chinese state’s use of "three-self" shows the language can serve political control.
Some argue a fourth "self", self-theologising (Hiebert), was neglected, and that interdependence is better than independence.
responses: Advocates reply that failures of implementation confirm rather than refute the principle.
Many now speak of partnership and interdependence while keeping local ownership.
consequences: Strong indigenous churches in Korea, Nigeria, Uganda and elsewhere.
Background to the Three-Self Patriotic Movement and its rejection by house churches.
Influence on Pentecostal mission strategy (Hodges, The Indigenous Church, 1953).

positions.name: Translatability and world Christianity (defence of mission against the colonial critique)
positions.oneLine: Christianity has no sacred language or single home culture; by translating Scripture into every vernacular, missions, despite colonial entanglements, empowered local peoples to receive the gospel on their own terms, producing a genuinely world Christianity.
coreClaims: Pentecost’s many tongues show that every language can carry revelation.
Translation relativises the missionary’s culture and dignifies the receptor culture.
Converts and local evangelists, not foreign missionaries, did most of the work of spreading the faith.
Missions often opposed colonial abuses and promoted literacy, education and civil society.
The colonial critique is real but incomplete: Christianity grew fastest after decolonisation.
positions.origin: Articulated by Andrew Walls (essays from the 1970s; The Missionary Movement in Christian History, 1996) and Lamin Sanneh (Translating the Message, 1989), developed by Kwame Bediako, Dana Robert, Brian Stanley (The Bible and the Flag, 1990) and quantitatively by Robert Woodberry (2012), in response to postcolonial critiques of mission.
strongestArguments: Unlike Islam’s Arabic Qur’an, Christian Scripture has always been translated, from the Septuagint to over 700 complete Bibles.
African and Asian Christianity exploded after missionaries and colonial rulers left (e.g. Africa from about 10 million Christians in 1900 to over 600 million today).
Mission schools trained many leaders of independence movements; Woodberry finds Protestant missions correlated with later democracy.
strongestObjections: Postcolonial historians (e.g. Jean and John Comaroff) argue that missions colonised consciousness, imposing Western norms in dress, family and economy.
Missionaries often depended on and legitimated colonial rule, and racial hierarchies persisted inside mission churches.
Emphasising agency of converts can minimise real harms such as residential schools in Canada and Australia.
responses: Walls and Sanneh do not deny complicity; they argue the message escaped its messengers, as seen in African Initiated Churches.
Stanley shows that relations between missions and empire were ambivalent, with missionaries both collaborating and opposing colonial interests.
consequences: Reframed missiology and church history as "world Christianity".
Encouraged study of African and Asian agency in Christian expansion.
Continuing debate with postcolonial and Indigenous critiques of mission.

positions.name: Missio Dei (the mission of God)
positions.oneLine: Mission is first God’s own activity: the Father sends the Son and the Spirit, and the triune God sends the Church; the Church does not have a mission so much as God’s mission has a Church.
coreClaims: Mission is rooted in the Trinity’s sending (John 20:21).
The Church is by nature missionary (Ad Gentes 2), not merely a sender of missionaries.
God is at work in the world beyond the Church, and the Church joins that work.
Mission includes proclamation, service, justice and care for creation (in broader versions).
Western societies are themselves mission fields (Newbigin, missional church).
positions.origin: Prepared by Karl Barth’s 1932 lecture on mission and the Trinity, crystallised at the IMC conference at Willingen (1952) and named by Karl Hartenstein; broadened in WCC circles (Uppsala 1968) toward "humanisation"; developed by David Bosch (Transforming Mission, 1991), Lesslie Newbigin and the "missional church" movement (Guder, 1998).
strongestArguments: Scripture presents mission as God’s initiative from Abraham to Pentecost, not a human programme.
It overcomes the split between "church" and "mission" and between home and foreign mission.
It places the Church in humility under God’s purposes, chastened after colonial missions.
strongestObjections: Evangelical critics argue that ecumenical versions dissolved mission into social and political action, losing evangelism (Uppsala 1968 controversy).
If God is active everywhere, the concept can become so broad that "if everything is mission, nothing is mission" (Stephen Neill).
Some theologians argue the Trinitarian "sending" analogy is used loosely.
responses: Advocates such as Bosch and Christopher Wright insist that missio Dei includes the proclamation of Christ as its heart.
Catholic and evangelical uses root it firmly in the Church’s proclamation and sacraments.
consequences: Integration of the IMC into the WCC (1961).
Missional church movement in Western post-Christendom contexts.
Common vocabulary across Catholic (Ad Gentes), Orthodox and Protestant missiology.

positions.name: Integral (holistic) mission
positions.oneLine: The gospel of the kingdom addresses the whole person and the whole of society, so evangelism and social responsibility are inseparable partners in the church’s mission.
coreClaims: Jesus proclaimed and enacted the kingdom: preaching, healing, feeding and confronting injustice (Luke 4:18–19).
Social action is not merely a bridge to evangelism but part of obedience to Christ.
Western evangelism was often captive to individualism and consumerism.
The church community itself embodies the gospel.
positions.origin: Raised by René Padilla and Samuel Escobar at Lausanne (1974) and developed by the Latin American Theological Fraternity (founded 1970); expressed in the Micah Declaration (2001) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010). Parallel Catholic emphasis in Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) and Pentecostal social engagement.
strongestArguments: Jesus’ own ministry combined word and deed inseparably.
Integral mission has credibility among the poor in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
It answers the charge that evangelicals cared only for souls.
strongestObjections: Some evangelicals fear it leads, as in parts of the ecumenical movement, to a social gospel that neglects conversion.
Critics argue social transformation belongs mainly to Christians’ vocations rather than the institutional church’s mission.
Liberationists sometimes see it as too cautious about structural and political change.
responses: Padilla and Stott insisted that evangelism remains central and that the kingdom is God’s work, not a human utopia.
They answer liberationist critics that the church must remain free from partisan ideologies.
consequences: Evangelical relief and development agencies (e.g. Tearfund, World Vision’s theological framework).
Micah Network (1999) and Cape Town Commitment (2010).
A distinctive Latin American evangelical theology.

positions.name: Particularism (exclusivism)
positions.oneLine: Jesus Christ is the unique and final revelation of God and the only saviour; other religions, however noble, are not paths to salvation, and the Church must call all people to faith in him.
coreClaims: Salvation is only through the person and work of Jesus Christ (Acts 4:12; John 14:6).
Other religions contain truths through general revelation and common grace but also error and rebellion; they do not save.
Truth claims of religions conflict and cannot all be correct (Netland).
Mission and evangelism are therefore urgent.
Particularists differ on whether explicit knowledge of Christ is required (restrictivism) or not (wider hope).
positions.origin: The dominant patristic, medieval and Reformation conviction; restated against pluralism by Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics I/2, §17, 1938), Hendrik Kraemer at Tambaram (1938), the Frankfurt Declaration (1970), the Lausanne Covenant (1974) and Lesslie Newbigin (1989).
strongestArguments: The New Testament repeatedly presents Christ as the unique and exclusive way.
Pluralism cannot account for the incarnation and resurrection as once-for-all events.
Contradictory claims (e.g. on God’s personhood, Christ’s death) cannot all be true.
strongestObjections: It seems to consign the majority of humanity, including those who never heard of Christ, to damnation (the problem of the unevangelised).
Pluralists argue that religious belief largely depends on birthplace, making exclusive claims arbitrary.
Its history is entangled with intolerance and coercion.
responses: Particularists answer that God’s justice and mercy toward the unevangelised can be trusted (Gen 18:25), and some hold a wider hope.
They argue that pluralism is itself a particular, Western-liberal claim, and that Christian particularity can coexist with respect and religious liberty (Newbigin).
consequences: Underpins evangelical, Pentecostal and much Orthodox and Catholic missionary motivation.
Lausanne movement and evangelical missiology.
Ongoing debates on interfaith relations and proselytism.

positions.name: Restrictivism
positions.oneLine: Only those who hear the gospel and explicitly believe in Christ (and, in the Catholic form, are joined to the Church) can be saved; those who die without such faith are lost.
coreClaims: Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Rom 10:14–17); without hearing there is no saving faith.
All are condemned in Adam and "without excuse" before general revelation (Rom 1:20).
There is no salvation outside the Church (Cyprian; Florence, 1442).
This fact gives mission its urgency.
positions.origin: Cyprian (c.256), Fulgentius of Ruspe, Boniface VIII’s Unam Sanctam (1302) and the Council of Florence (1442); widely held by Reformation and modern Protestants; in strict Catholic form taught by Leonard Feeney and rejected by Rome (1949); defended by evangelicals such as Ronald Nash (Is Jesus the Only Savior?, 1994).
strongestArguments: Romans 10 explicitly ties salvation to hearing and believing the gospel.
The Book of Acts shows even devout seekers (Cornelius) needing to hear about Christ.
It preserves the urgency of mission that drove Carey and Taylor.
strongestObjections: It seems to make salvation depend on geographical and historical accident, which critics call incompatible with God’s love (1 Tim 2:4).
Old Testament believers and "holy pagans" (Melchizedek, Job, Rahab) were saved without knowing Jesus by name.
Catholic teaching since 1949 and Vatican II has rejected the strict reading.
responses: Restrictivists answer that Old Testament believers trusted God’s promised redeemer, a special revelation unavailable to modern unevangelised peoples.
They argue that God justly condemns sinners and that the remedy is mission, not speculation about other ways.
consequences: Strong motive for evangelical and earlier Catholic missions.
Moral and theological objections that fuelled inclusivism and pluralism.
The Feeney controversy and Catholic clarification (1949).

positions.name: Wider hope (accessibilism)
positions.oneLine: Salvation is only through Christ, but God may save those who never heard the gospel if they respond in faith to the light they receive, or by encountering Christ at or after death.
coreClaims: Christ is the only saviour (ontological necessity) but explicit knowledge of him may not be required (epistemological openness).
God desires all to be saved (1 Tim 2:4) and judges according to the light people have (Rom 2:6–16).
Old Testament and pagan believers (Abel, Enoch, Job, Melchizedek) were saved by faith without knowing Jesus.
Some propose that the unevangelised meet Christ after death (1 Pet 3:19; 4:6).
positions.origin: Anticipated by Justin and Zwingli (who hoped to meet Socrates in heaven), John Wesley, C. S. Lewis (The Last Battle, 1956) and Norman Anderson; argued by Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God’s Mercy, 1992) and John Sanders (No Other Name, 1992); post-mortem versions by George Lindbeck and Gabriel Fackre.
strongestArguments: It holds together Christ’s uniqueness and God’s universal saving will.
Scripture includes believers outside Israel who knew God without the Law or Christ.
It avoids the apparent arbitrariness of restrictivism without embracing pluralism.
strongestObjections: Restrictivists argue it undermines the urgency of mission and contradicts Romans 10.
There is no clear biblical example of someone saved through another religion after Christ came (Cornelius still needed Peter).
Pluralists see it as a half-way house that still privileges Christianity.
responses: Advocates answer that mission brings the fullness of salvation, assurance and the Church, not merely escape from hell.
They claim no certainty about how many are saved, only hope grounded in God’s character.
consequences: A significant minority view among evangelicals and Wesleyans.
Controversy in the Evangelical Theological Society in the 1990s (open theism debates with Pinnock and Sanders).

positions.name: Inclusivism ("anonymous Christians")
positions.oneLine: Christ is the unique saviour of all, but his grace is at work beyond the visible Church, including in and through other religions, so that sincere non-Christians may be saved by Christ without knowing him explicitly.
coreClaims: God’s universal saving will (1 Tim 2:4) means grace is offered to every human being.
Other religions may contain "seeds of the Word" and "rays of truth" and mediate grace in a provisional way.
All who are saved are saved by Christ and ordered toward the Church.
Dialogue and mission are both necessary: dialogue respects truth in others; mission makes explicit what is anonymous.
positions.origin: Roots in Justin’s Logos theology and the fulfilment theology of J. N. Farquhar (The Crown of Hinduism, 1913); formulated by Karl Rahner (1961) and taught in Lumen Gentium 16 and Nostra Aetate (1964–65); developed by John Paul II (Assisi prayer meetings, 1986; Redemptoris Missio, 1990) and Jacques Dupuis.
strongestArguments: It integrates the scriptural witness to Christ’s uniqueness with texts about God’s universal light.
It recognises the evident goodness and holiness in many adherents of other faiths.
It has become official Catholic teaching through an ecumenical council.
strongestObjections: Particularists argue it weakens the necessity of explicit faith and of mission.
Pluralists and adherents of other faiths find "anonymous Christian" patronising, as if a Buddhist were a Christian without knowing it.
Critics ask why, if other religions mediate grace, the Church is needed at all.
responses: Rahner answered that the label is a Christian self-description of hope, not a claim imposed on others.
Catholic teaching (Redemptoris Missio, Dominus Iesus) insists that dialogue does not replace mission and that the Church remains the ordinary means of salvation.
consequences: Vatican II teaching on salvation and the religions.
Formal interreligious dialogue (Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue, 1964; Assisi 1986).
Debates over Jacques Dupuis and Asian Catholic theologies.

positions.name: Religious pluralism
positions.oneLine: The major world religions are equally valid, culturally conditioned responses to one ultimate divine Reality, and none, including Christianity, is uniquely true or uniquely saving.
coreClaims: The Real (God) lies beyond all human concepts; religions are different human responses to it.
Salvation is the transformation from self-centredness to Reality-centredness, visible in many traditions.
Incarnation language is mythological or metaphorical rather than literal (Hick).
Dialogue and cooperation for justice should replace conversion (Knitter).
positions.origin: Precedents in Enlightenment deism, Lessing’s Nathan the Wise (1779), Ernst Troeltsch and Wilfred Cantwell Smith; formulated by John Hick (God and the Universe of Faiths, 1973; An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) and The Myth of Christian Uniqueness (Hick and Knitter, 1987); Asian voices include Stanley Samartha and Raimon Panikkar.
strongestArguments: Religious belief correlates strongly with birthplace, which seems to make exclusive truth claims arbitrary.
Saintliness and moral transformation appear across religions.
It fosters peace and respect in religiously plural societies.
strongestObjections: Most Christians judge it incompatible with the New Testament’s witness to Christ’s uniqueness and with the creeds.
Critics (Newbigin, D’Costa) argue it is itself an exclusivist, Western-Kantian position that redefines all religions in its own terms.
Adherents of other religions often reject the claim that their faith is "one path" to the same Reality.
responses: Pluralists reply that every theory has a vantage point, but theirs is more inclusive and humble.
They argue that Christian commitment can be wholehearted without being exclusive ("love language" of devotion).
consequences: Influence in liberal Protestant seminaries and interfaith organisations.
Catholic disciplinary responses (Dominus Iesus, 2000; notifications on Dupuis and others).
Strong evangelical apologetic responses.

positions.name: Religious liberty as a Christian principle
positions.oneLine: Because faith must be free and every person bears God’s image, no one may be coerced in religion by the state or others; the church proclaims by persuasion, and states should protect freedom of religion for all.
coreClaims: Genuine faith cannot be compelled (Tertullian: it is not part of religion to compel religion).
Christ’s kingdom is not of this world; its weapons are spiritual (John 18:36; 2 Cor 10:4).
Religious freedom is grounded in human dignity and the nature of faith (Dignitatis Humanae).
Freedom includes worship, teaching, changing one’s religion and corporate church life.
positions.origin: Early apologists (Tertullian, Lactantius) pleaded for freedom; after Constantine and Augustine’s acceptance of coercion against Donatists it faded. Anabaptists (Hubmaier, On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them, 1524), Baptists (Thomas Helwys, 1612; Roger Williams, 1644), Quakers (William Penn) and Enlightenment thinkers revived it; the Catholic Church embraced it in Dignitatis Humanae (1965) and the WCC in 1948.
strongestArguments: Coerced faith is not faith; Jesus never forced belief.
Centuries of religious wars and persecutions show the evil of coercion, including by Christians against Christians.
It protects Christians themselves, who are today among the most persecuted religious groups.
strongestObjections: Before 1965 much Catholic teaching (e.g. Pius IX’s Syllabus of Errors, 1864) held that error has no rights and the state should favour the true religion.
Traditionalists argue Dignitatis Humanae contradicts earlier magisterial teaching.
Some argue that unlimited liberty enables proselytism and social fragmentation, a concern voiced in some Orthodox and Muslim-majority contexts.
responses: Defenders answer that development of doctrine, rooted in human dignity and the freedom of the act of faith, explains the change (Murray, Ratzinger).
They distinguish legitimate witness from coercive or manipulative proselytism.
consequences: Catholic support for democracy and human rights after 1965.
Christian advocacy for persecuted minorities worldwide.
Constitutional protections such as the US First Amendment and Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).

controversies.question: May Chinese Christians honour their ancestors and Confucius, and call God "Tian" or "Shangdi"?
controversies.title: The Chinese Rites controversy
controversies.summary: For more than a century Jesuits, Dominicans, Franciscans, popes and Chinese emperors argued whether Confucian and ancestral rites were civil honours compatible with the faith or idolatrous worship, and whether Chinese terms could name God. Rome’s ban (1704–1742) crippled the mission; its reversal (1939) prefigured modern inculturation.

sides.name: Jesuit accommodation
sides.steelman: The Chinese classics already knew the Lord on High, and honouring ancestors and Confucius is filial piety and civic respect, not worship of gods. Paul quoted the poets of Athens; we must speak to China in its own noble language. To forbid these rites is to tell the Chinese that becoming Christian means ceasing to be Chinese, and to close the empire to the gospel.
counterArguments: Rites include offerings and prayers to spirits

sides.name: Mendicant and papal prohibition
sides.steelman: Whatever the scholars say, ordinary Chinese offer food, incense and prayers to the spirits of the dead and to Confucius, expecting blessings. To tolerate such rites is to tolerate idolatry, and to call God by names that the Chinese use for heaven or a deity confuses the Creator with creation. The purity of the faith cannot be traded for imperial favour.

timeline.text: Ricci admitted to Beijing.
Propaganda Fide, on Dominican complaints, first condemns the rites; a 1656 decree permits them on Jesuit representation.
Kangxi’s edict of toleration.
Clement XI condemns the rites; papal legate Tournon’s mission fails.
Kangxi, reading the papal bull Ex illa die (1715), bans Christian preaching.
Ex quo singulari makes the ban final.
Pius XII’s Plane compertum est permits Chinese Catholics to honour Confucius and ancestors.

resolution.text: Rome forbade the rites in 1704–1742 and permitted them in 1939, judging that their meaning had become civil; Vatican II’s respect for cultures vindicated much of the accommodation approach. Protestant churches in China, Korea and Japan still debate ancestral rites, often forbidding bowing at ancestral tablets.

consequences: Imperial restrictions on Christianity in China (1721–1840s).
Contributed to the suppression of the Jesuits (1773).
A paradigm case for later theories of inculturation.

controversies.question: Can people who never hear of Christ, or who follow other religions, be saved?
controversies.title: Christ and the religions: restrictivism, wider hope, inclusivism and pluralism
controversies.summary: Christians agree that Christ is Lord and saviour but disagree on what this means for the billions who have lived and died without hearing the gospel or who sincerely follow other faiths. The debate intensified with global encounter, Vatican II and the rise of religiously plural societies.

sides.name: Restrictivism
sides.steelman: Scripture says faith comes by hearing and that there is no other name. All have sinned and are without excuse. If people could be saved without the gospel, the apostles’ urgency would make no sense. Our task is not to speculate about other ways but to go and tell.

sides.name: Wider hope / accessibilism
sides.steelman: Christ alone saves, but God’s mercy is wider than our knowledge. Abel, Job and Melchizedek were saved by faith without knowing Jesus’ name; God will judge each by the light they had. We may hope, while still telling everyone the good news in full.

sides.name: Inclusivism
sides.steelman: The Word enlightens every person coming into the world. God’s grace can reach people through what is true and holy in their own traditions, always as the grace of Christ and oriented toward his Church. Dialogue honours that grace; mission brings it to fullness.

sides.name: Pluralism
sides.steelman: It is implausible that the God of love would confine salvation to one tradition that most humans never encountered. The great faiths produce saints and transform lives; they are different human responses to the one Real. Humility, not superiority, should mark our relations with them.

timeline.text: Justin speaks of seeds of the Word among the Greeks.
Cyprian: no salvation outside the Church.
Florence’s Cantate Domino gives the strict reading.
Kraemer’s particularism debated at Tambaram.
Holy Office rejects Feeney’s strict view.
Vatican II’s Nostra Aetate and Lumen Gentium 16.
Lausanne Covenant rejects universalism and syncretism.
Pinnock and Sanders argue for a wider hope.
Dominus Iesus rejects pluralist theologies.

resolution.text: Unresolved. The Catholic Church officially holds inclusivism within Christ’s unique mediation; Orthodox churches generally leave the fate of others to God’s mercy; evangelicals divide between restrictivism and wider hope; pluralism is found mainly in liberal Protestantism and academic theology.

consequences: Shapes motivation and methods of mission.
Framework for interreligious dialogue bodies.
Debates within evangelicalism over inclusivism and universalism.

controversies.question: Was modern Christian mission an instrument of colonial empire or the seed of indigenous world Christianity?
controversies.title: Mission and colonialism: critique and defence
controversies.summary: Missions accompanied Spanish, Portuguese, British, French and other empires, and critics charge them with cultural imperialism and complicity in conquest. Defenders and many historians argue that missionaries also resisted abuses, translated Scripture into local languages and empowered indigenous Christians who soon outgrew missionary control.

sides.name: The colonial critique
sides.steelman: Missionaries arrived with gunboats, treaties and racial hierarchies. They condemned local religions, dress and family structures as heathen, served colonial administrations through schools and hospitals, and kept indigenous Christians subordinate (as with Bishop Crowther). Residential schools, forced conversions in the Americas and the Requerimiento show that the cross and the sword often travelled together.

sides.name: Translation and indigenous agency
sides.steelman: The colonial story is real but not the whole story. Missionaries translated the Bible into hundreds of languages, gave peoples written literatures and schools, and often fought colonial injustice. Above all, African, Asian and Latin American Christians received the faith on their own terms, made it their own and spread it far beyond missionary control, which is why Christianity grew fastest after empire ended.
counterArguments: Converts’ agency does not excuse missionaries

timeline.text: Spanish conquest and the beginning of colonial missions in the Americas.
Valladolid debate on Indigenous rights.
Evangelical campaign secures abolition of the British slave trade.
Crowther consecrated first African Anglican bishop.
Edinburgh conference, dominated by Western delegates.
William Wade Harris’s independent mass movement in West Africa.
China’s Three-Self Patriotic Movement severs foreign ties.
Sanneh’s Translating the Message reframes the debate.

resolution.text: Historians now generally describe a mixed and ambivalent relationship between missions and empire. Churches have apologised for specific harms (e.g. Canadian residential schools, papal apology 2022), while world Christianity scholarship stresses indigenous agency.

consequences: Apologies and reconciliation processes with Indigenous peoples.
Shift to partnership and Global South leadership in mission.
Rise of world Christianity as a field of study.

people.name: Henry Venn
roles: honorary secretary of the Church Missionary Society (1841–1872)
people.summary: Evangelical mission strategist who directed the Church Missionary Society for three decades and formulated the goal of "self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending" native churches, after which the foreign mission should withdraw ("the euthanasia of a mission"). He championed the consecration of Samuel Ajayi Crowther as the first African Anglican bishop (1864).

people.name: John Livingstone Nevius
people.summary: Missionary in Shandong whose Methods of Mission Work (1886) urged self-supporting, self-propagating churches led by unpaid local leaders. Adopted by Presbyterian missionaries in Korea after his visit in 1890, the "Nevius plan" is credited with shaping the strongly indigenous Korean Protestant church.
keyIdeas: Bible study system for lay leaders

people.name: Roberto de Nobili
people.summary: Italian Jesuit in Madurai who adopted the dress, diet and lifestyle of a Brahmin sannyasi, learned Tamil and Sanskrit, and allowed converts to keep caste customs he judged social rather than religious. His method, contested by fellow missionaries, was approved by Gregory XV (1623) and later restricted in the Malabar Rites controversy (1704–1744).
keyIdeas: Distinction between civil and religious customs

people.name: Hendrik Kraemer
roles: first director of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey
people.summary: Dutch Reformed lay missiologist and scholar of Islam in Java whose The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World (1938), written for the Tambaram conference, argued under Barth’s influence for "biblical realism": the radical discontinuity between the gospel and all religions.

people.name: Lesslie Newbigin
roles: bishop in the Church of South India
people.summary: Scottish missionary who became a bishop of the united Church of South India (1947), helped integrate the International Missionary Council into the WCC (1961), and in retirement in Birmingham argued that the West itself had become a mission field. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) defended Christian particularity against pluralism and called the congregation "the hermeneutic of the gospel".
keyIdeas: Missio Dei and mission to the West
Congregation as hermeneutic of the gospel

people.name: John Hick
people.summary: British philosopher, originally an evangelical Presbyterian, whose experience of multi-faith Birmingham led him to call for a "Copernican revolution" in theology (God and the Universe of Faiths, 1973): the great religions are diverse human responses to one ultimate Reality. His An Interpretation of Religion (1989) is the classic statement of religious pluralism. He was later outside historic orthodox Christology (The Myth of God Incarnate, 1977).
keyIdeas: Copernican revolution in theology of religions

people.name: Lamin Sanneh
people.summary: Gambian-born scholar, a convert from Islam, whose Translating the Message (1989) argued that Christianity’s commitment to vernacular Bible translation made it a force for indigenous cultural renewal rather than simply a tool of colonialism. Whose Religion Is Christianity? (2003) described the emergence of world Christianity.

people.name: C. René Padilla
roles: leader of the Latin American Theological Fraternity
people.summary: Ecuadorian-born Argentine Baptist theologian whose address at Lausanne (1974), with Samuel Escobar’s, challenged North American evangelism as culturally captive and called for "integral mission" (misión integral), joining evangelism and social responsibility under the kingdom of God.
keyIdeas: Kingdom of God as framework of mission

people.name: Leonard Feeney
roles: founder of the Slaves of the Immaculate Heart of Mary
people.summary: Boston Jesuit who taught a strict reading of "outside the Church there is no salvation", denying salvation to any who die without explicit membership in the Catholic Church. The Holy Office’s letter to Archbishop Cushing (1949) rejected his interpretation; he was excommunicated for disobedience (1953) and reconciled in 1972.

events.title: Dignitatis Humanae
events.summary: Vatican II’s declaration on religious freedom (7 December 1965) affirms that every person has a right, grounded in human dignity, to be free from coercion in religious matters, privately and publicly, within just limits; it was largely drafted with John Courtney Murray and contested by a conservative minority.
causes: American and Eastern European bishops’ experience
consequences: Catholic support for religious liberty and democracy (the "third wave" of democratisation)
Traditionalist objections (Lefebvre)

events.title: Willingen missionary conference
events.summary: Meeting of the International Missionary Council at Willingen, Germany, which grounded mission in the sending activity of the triune God; the term missio Dei, popularised soon afterwards by Karl Hartenstein, became the central concept of 20th-century ecumenical missiology.
consequences: Missio Dei theology
Integration of the IMC into the WCC (1961)

events.title: Holy Office letter on the Feeney case
events.summary: The Holy Office’s letter to Archbishop Richard Cushing of Boston rejects Leonard Feeney’s strict interpretation of "outside the Church there is no salvation", teaching that those invincibly ignorant of the Church may be saved by implicit desire informed by perfect charity.

events.title: Ex quo singulari bans the Chinese Rites
events.summary: Benedict XIV’s bull Ex quo singulari confirms Clement XI’s condemnations (1704, 1715) of Chinese ancestral and Confucian rites and of the terms Tian and Shangdi for God, and imposes an oath on missionaries; Omnium sollicitudinum (1744) does the same for the Malabar Rites in India. Pius XII lifts the ban in 1939 (Plane compertum est).
causes: Dominican and Franciscan objections to Jesuit accommodation
consequences: Kangxi’s and Yongzheng’s restrictions on Christianity
Weakening of the China mission until the 19th century

works.title: An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens
works.summary: Carey argues that the Great Commission still binds the church, surveys the world’s population and religions, and proposes a missionary society.
works.significance: Manifesto of the modern Protestant missionary movement.

works.title: The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu Shiyi)
works.summary: Dialogue between a Western and a Chinese scholar arguing from reason and the Confucian classics for the Lord of Heaven, the soul and moral cultivation.
works.significance: Classic of Jesuit accommodation, read by Chinese, Korean and Japanese literati.

works.title: The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World
works.summary: Preparatory volume for the Tambaram conference on the relation of the gospel to the religions.
works.significance: Classic statement of discontinuity between revelation and religion.

works.title: God and the Universe of Faiths
works.summary: Essays proposing a "Copernican revolution" placing God, not Christianity, at the centre of the universe of faiths.
works.significance: Founding text of Christian religious pluralism.

works.title: Dignitatis Humanae (Declaration on Religious Freedom)
works.summary: Declaration on the right of persons and communities to social and civil freedom in religious matters.
works.significance: Marked the Catholic Church’s embrace of religious liberty.

works.title: Dominus Iesus
works.summary: Declaration of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on the unique and universal saving role of Christ and the Church.
works.significance: Major Catholic response to religious pluralism.

works.title: Translating the Message: The Missionary Impact on Culture
works.summary: Historical study of Bible translation and vernacular renewal from the early church to modern Africa.
works.significance: Reframed the debate on mission and colonialism.

quotes.text: We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared above that He is the Word of whom every race of men were partakers; and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them ...

Cyprian argued that baptism and salvation belong only to the one Church, since there is no salvation outside the Church (salus extra ecclesiam non est), so that even martyrdom outside her unity cannot save.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Cyprian, Epistle 72 (73), To Jubaianus, 21

quotes.text: ... for there is no doubt that it is impossible to efface every thing at once from their obdurate minds; because he who endeavours to ascend to the highest place, rises by degrees or steps, and not by leaps.
quotes.citation: Gregory the Great, letter to Abbot Mellitus (601), in Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30 (tr. J. A. Giles, 1847)

quotes.text: Ricci argued that the ancient Chinese classics already knew the Lord on High (Shangdi), whom Christians call the Lord of Heaven, and that later Neo-Confucian materialism, not Confucius, had obscured this truth.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Ricci, The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (1603), ch. 2

quotes.text: Carey contended that the command to teach all nations was not confined to the apostles but binds Christians in every age, and that believers are obliged to use every lawful means, forming societies, sending missionaries and giving money, for the conversion of the heathen.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Carey, An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians (1792), section 1

quotes.text: Venn taught that the aim of a mission is a native church that is self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending; once that is reached the missionary should move on, which he called "the euthanasia of a mission".
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Henry Venn, CMS minutes on native church organisation (1851, 1861)

quotes.text: Kraemer held that the revelation in Christ stands in radical discontinuity with every religion, including empirical Christianity; religions are human achievements, noble and sinful, judged and yet sought by God’s self-disclosure.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Kraemer, The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World (1938), chs. 4–5

quotes.text: Rahner argued that because God wills all to be saved, grace must be offered to every person, and that non-Christians who accept it in conscience, even through their own religions, may be called "anonymous Christians" saved by Christ though they do not know him by name.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Karl Rahner, "Christianity and the Non-Christian Religions" (lecture 1961; Theological Investigations vol. 5)

quotes.text: The Council taught that the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, regarding with sincere respect their ways of life and teachings, which often reflect a ray of the Truth that enlightens all people, while it proclaims Christ as the way, the truth and the life.

Dignitatis Humanae declares that the human person has a right to religious freedom, meaning immunity from coercion by individuals, groups or any human power, so that no one is forced to act against conscience in religious matters, a right grounded in the dignity of the person known through revelation and reason.

Hick called for a Copernican revolution in theology: instead of placing Christianity at the centre with other religions revolving around it, Christians should recognise that God (the Real) is at the centre and that all the great faiths revolve around and respond to that one divine reality.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of John Hick, God and the Universe of Faiths (1973), ch. 9

quotes.text: Dominus Iesus insists that Jesus Christ is the unique and universal mediator of salvation and that the Church is necessary for salvation; it rejects theories that treat religions as equal paths, while affirming that non-Christians can receive grace, though objectively in a gravely deficient situation compared with those in the Church.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Dominus Iesus 13–22 (6 August 2000), signed by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger as Prefect

quotes.text: Pinnock argued that God’s boundless generosity means everyone has access to saving grace; people like Job, Melchizedek and the "holy pagans" of Scripture show that those who respond in faith to the light they have can be saved by Christ, even without hearing of him.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Clark Pinnock, A Wideness in God’s Mercy (1992), chs. 1 and 5

quotes.text: Sanneh argued that by translating the Bible into local languages, missions made the vernacular a vehicle of revelation, thereby relativising Western culture and stimulating indigenous renewal and resistance that often outran missionary and colonial control.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Lamin Sanneh, Translating the Message (1989), Introduction and ch. 6

quotes.text: Padilla argued that evangelism and social responsibility are inseparable dimensions of the gospel of the kingdom, and that much missionary preaching was captive to a Western consumerist culture that offered cheap grace without discipleship.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of C. René Padilla, "Evangelism and the World", Lausanne Congress (1974)
